7.0.s.en: (1) The reducing of the number of soldiers

7.0.0.en: The well of Harod: a spring of water about 1.5 km southeast of Jezreel and northwest of Mount Gilead.

7.0.1.en: The hill of Moreh: the valley lying between Mount Gilboa (Gilead) on the south and Mount Tabor on the north, about 4 miles from the well of Harod (Map 12). Gideon made sure that the Lord stood by him in his war against the Midianites, so he gathered the men of his army and they made their camp at the well of Harod in readiness to face the enemies, while the camp of the Midianites was to the north of them at the hill of Moreh.

7.1.0.en: God knew that His people might become proud if He gave them victory over the Midianites, and ascribe the victory to the greatness of their number, so He spoke to Gideon to reduce the number of soldiers with him, although they were far fewer than the number of the Midianites. This is a proof that strength is from God and that the fewness of His people's soldiers does not matter to Him.

7.2.0.en: Mount Gilead: it lies in the valley of Jezreel west of the Jordan River, near the well of Harod. It is not the Mount Gilead which lies east of the Jordan River.

7.2.1.en: The Lord reminded Gideon of the law of war which He gave to Moses in the Book of Deuteronomy, which is that the leaders of the people proclaim among the soldiers that everyone who is fearful of the war should return to his house (Deut 20:5-8). So at Gideon's proclamation twenty-two thousand returned, and only ten thousand remained with him.

7.3.0.en: I will try them: I will test them and prove them by what will happen to them.

7.3.1.en: Despite the smallness of the number that remained after Gideon's proclamation, as the previous verse relates, the Lord found that the number of ten thousand was still large and that they must be reduced. For this reason the Lord commanded Gideon to bring them down to the water, that is, the water of the well of Harod beside which they were encamped, to drink, and He would designate for him those whom he should take with him to the war and those whom he should not.

7.4.0.en: Every one that lappeth of the water with his tongue, as a dog lappeth: that is, he drinks the water as a dog drinks, by sucking the water from the spring directly with his mouth or quickly with the palm of his hand.

7.4.1.en: The men went down to the water to drink, and the Lord commanded Gideon to watch how they drank: everyone who takes the water in his hand to his mouth to drink quickly he was to put on one side, and everyone who drinks the water from the spring with his mouth while kneeling, that is, who drinks quietly and gives himself a chance to wash and rest, he was to put on another side.

7.5.0.en: The number of those who took the water in the palm to the mouth was only three hundred men, while the rest were of those who bowed down upon their knees to drink.

7.6.0.en: After this sifting the Lord carried out among the men of war, He declared to Gideon that by the three hundred men who took the water in the palm to the mouth He would defeat the Midianites and deliver his people from them, and even deliver them into their hands so that they might carry out just judgment upon them, and that the others should return to their houses.

7.6.1.en: Kneeling on the knees to drink water directly with the mouth shows a lack of watchfulness and attention to what may happen before them, and takes longer than taking water by hand to the mouth, which gives the enemies a chance to attack with no readiness on the part of the one drinking in this way. But the one who takes the water by hand to the mouth does so in a shorter time, besides keeping his eyes directed forward, that is, toward the enemy, so he remains on his guard against him while he drinks.

7.7.1.en: The three hundred men whom the Lord designated prepared themselves, taking their trumpets and the food they needed on their way, while Gideon sent the rest to their homes. Gideon and his men were in a place a little higher than the spot where the Midianites were encamped.

7.7.2.en: The standing of the three hundred men on the high place made it easy for them to see the very great numbers of the Midianites in the valley, so they felt their weakness and sought God, and by this the power of God that would give them victory appears.

7.7.3.en: God wants you to be always ready and watchful in your spiritual warfare with Satan, so that he does not seize the chance of your heedlessness and make you fall into sin. So be on guard and keep away from the sources of your sin, and fill your emptiness with constructive spiritual thoughts, and seek God's help, and you will secure your victory over your enemies.

7.8.0.en: God wanted to give Gideon a new sign to reassure him that He was with him and would help him achieve the victory, so He asked him on that night to go down to where the camp of the Midianites was in order to show him the new sign, and informed him that He would deliver the Midianites into his hand. The Lord said it in the past tense, "I have delivered it", to confirm that the matter must be accomplished.

7.9.0.en: To increase Gideon's assurance, God sent him with one of his faithful servants named "Phurah" to spy out the camp of the Midianites himself. Spying is a well-known thing in wars in order to learn the strength of the enemies, but God intended to show Gideon His power and His superiority over the enemies.

7.10.0.en: The armed men that were in the host: the soldiers prepared for war who were in the camp. The Lord had a purpose in Gideon's going down to the camp of the Midianites, which was that Gideon should hear a conversation going on among some of them, and the content of this conversation would encourage him more and reassure him of the achievement of the victory. The Lord knew what they would say and Gideon would hear, so that he would be more and more encouraged and not fear to face them. Gideon obeyed the Lord's command and went down, he and his servant, to the rear of the Midianite camp, without penetrating into their ranks so that they would not notice him.

7.11.0.en: God repeated what was mentioned in (ch. 6:5), likening the enemy army in its multitude to grasshoppers, and their camels, which were among the essentials of war in that time, to the sand of the sea in their multitude.

7.12.0.en: The new sign the Lord wanted to give Gideon to encourage him more was the content of a dream that one of the enemy soldiers had seen and related to one of his companions while Gideon was there listening to their conversation. The content of the dream was that he saw a loaf of barley bread rolling on the ground in the camp of the Midianites, and it struck their tents and threw them down and turned them upside down.

7.13.0.en: No sooner had the soldier finished telling his dream than his companion, by God's intervention, interpreted the dream to him: that the loaf of barley bread signifies the sword of Gideon, to whom the Lord gives strength and victory over the Midianites, so that he crushes their army. And the barley loaf is the weakest kind of bread and is the food of the poor; it resembles weak Gideon, but because God is with him he is able to defeat the many enemies.

7.13.1.en: Thank God for every encouragement He sends you and every grace you receive, and your enjoyment of it will increase, and God will pour out on you more mercies, so that you live assured and joyful.

7.14.0.en: When Gideon heard the dream and its interpretation, he was encouraged and became certain that God was with him, so he worshiped God in thanksgiving and returned to the camp of the children of Israel and roused them, saying: Arise, for the Lord has delivered the host of Midian into your hand. Here Gideon's humility appears, for he ascribes the victory to his soldiers, saying that the Midianites were delivered into your hand, in order to encourage them also.

7.14.1.en: God intervened at the last moment to remove the anxiety from Gideon's heart, that is, on the last night before he began the war. So be assured that God is near to you and will intervene at the right time to encourage you and give you victory over your enemies.

7.15.0.en: Gideon divided his army into three companies, spread over a wider area so as to make the enemies imagine that their numbers were greater than they really were, and commanded them that each soldier should carry a trumpet in his right hand to blow it at the time he would indicate to them, and in his other hand carry an empty pitcher with a lamp placed inside it.

7.15.1.en: Our reliance on the Lord in the steps we take does not mean not planning and organizing them. We must strive and arrange our affairs in the best possible way, and God completes and crowns this effort with blessing and success.

7.16.0.en: Gideon told them that he would be at the head of one of the three companies, and would advance to the edge of the camp occupied by the Midianites, and commanded them to do as they saw him do.

7.17.0.en: The plan was that when he blew the trumpets with his company, all the men of the other two companies should blow their trumpets while surrounding the camp and shout "For the Lord and for Gideon", that is, that the Lord would draw His sword, and the sword of Gideon His servant, against the enemies. As for the rest of the military plan which Gideon told his soldiers, it is mentioned in the following verses.

7.17.1.en: v. 19 The watch: the middle one: it is the second part of the night, which was divided into three parts, each of four hours, from six o'clock in the evening to six o'clock in the morning by our present reckoning. At midnight Gideon moved with his company, made up of a hundred soldiers, to the edge of the Midianite camp, and the Midianites were asleep and had assigned some soldiers to guard their camp. Gideon's company began to carry out the plan by blowing the trumpets and breaking the pitchers, throwing them hard on the ground, and at the same time showing the torches that they had been hiding inside them.

7.18.0.en: The sword of the Lord and of Gideon: that is, the Lord will unleash His sword and the sword of Gideon upon the enemies.

7.18.1.en: The other two companies imitated them, carrying out Gideon's orders when he told them that as they saw him do, so they should do, all crying out "The sword of the Lord and of Gideon." And they blew the trumpets and broke the pitchers and attacked the enemies, blowing the trumpets in their right hands with the lamps in their left hands, which greatly alarmed the enemies.

7.19.0.en: After they carried out the plan according to Gideon's instructions, they stood firm around the camp of the enemies, while these were terrified by the sounds of the trumpets and the sound made by the breaking of the pitchers in a single moment, and they were afraid of the fire of the torches, imagining that they were new weapons that would destroy them, so they fled before Gideon's soldiers, for the Lord cast terror into their hearts.

7.19.1.en: As the enemies were terrified by the sound of the trumpets and the breaking of the pitchers, so the soldiers of the enemy of good are terrified by the sign of the Cross and by our regular practice of the sacrament of Communion of the Body and Blood of the Lord, by which we abide in the Lord Jesus, so that serpents and scorpions and all the power of the enemy cannot prevail over us.

7.20.0.en: The three hundred soldiers continued to blow the trumpets so as to make the enemy imagine that they were a multitude of fighting men and not merely a small number of soldiers, so panic seized the enemy soldiers and in their confusion they began to kill one another, thinking that they were killing Gideon's men, and then they discovered that their comrades had been killed, from their cries, and thought that Gideon's men had killed them, so their fear increased and they hastened to flee. Chaos prevailed among them, each of them trying to save himself and flee from the field of battle, so they were scattered and withdrew to several towns, "Beth-shittah", "Zererath", the border of "Abel-meholah" and "Tabbath", and these places lie in the east of the valley of Jezreel as far as the Jordan River.

7.21.0.en: The tribes that lived in the regions near the field of battle saw the defeat of the Midianites and the flight of their men, so the men of war of the tribes of Naphtali, Asher and Manasseh were roused and went out to pursue those who fled from the army of the Midianites.

7.22.0.en: Take before them the waters: seize the gatherings of water of the Jordan River in order to block the way of those fleeing from the Midianite army, lest they escape by swimming in the waters of the Jordan.

7.22.1.en: Beth-barah: a city on the eastern bank of the Jordan River (Map 11). The tribe of Ephraim lived in the mountainous lands in the middle of the land of Canaan. So Gideon asked them to come down to the plains and take control of the gatherings of water connected with the Jordan River, to prevent the Midianites from crossing the river to its eastern bank to return to their country. The tribe of Ephraim carried out Gideon's request and by this prevented the Midianites from escaping, which would perhaps have helped them to reorganize their ranks in their own lands and return to fight the children of Israel anew.

7.23.0.en: The rock of Oreb: a place on the western bank of the Jordan River.

7.23.1.en: The Ephraimites succeeded in capturing the enemy soldiers during their retreat in flight from the field of battle, and seized two of their princes, "Oreb" and "Zeeb", and killed the prince Oreb on a rock which they named "the rock of Oreb", and killed the prince Zeeb at an olive press in which he was perhaps hiding and called it by his name, "the winepress of Zeeb", and they sent the heads of the two slain princes to Gideon to bring him good news.

7.23.2.en: The continuing of the victories over the Midianites (1) Ephraim's anger at Gideon (vv. 1-3) 1 And the men of Ephraim said unto him, Why hast thou served us thus, that thou calledst us not, when thou wentest to fight with the Midianites? And they did chide with him sharply. 2 And he said unto them, What have I done now in comparison of you? Is not the gleaning of the grapes of Ephraim better than the vintage of Abi-ezer? 3 God hath delivered into your hands the princes of Midian, Oreb and Zeeb: and what was I able to do in comparison of you? Then their anger was abated toward him, when he had said that.

8.0.0.en: Gideon's request to the tribe of Ephraim was to take control of the gatherings of the waters of the Jordan to prevent the fleeing Midianites from crossing to their country, as came at the end of the previous chapter; this request came almost at the end of the war. Although Ephraim answered Gideon's call, they held it against him that he had not summoned them from the beginning to the war against the Midianites, and they were angry with him, for they considered themselves among the greatest and most important of the tribes, and after the killing of the princes Oreb and Zeeb and the killing of many of the Midianite army, they became proud, especially as they have a readiness for pride because of their great number, although they are not as brave as the rest of the tribes, but they object a great deal because of their pride.

8.1.0.en: Is not the gleaning of the grapes of Ephraim better than the vintage of Abi-ezer: the gleaning is the fruit that remains on the tree after the fruit is gathered, and the vintage is the fruit that has been gathered. So the gleaning is the leavings compared with the vintage.

8.1.1.en: Here Gideon's wisdom in leadership appeared, and he met the matter with gentleness and humility, so he gave them back the greater credit for achieving the victory, telling them that what he had done in the war cannot be compared with the great work they had done. And he went further in his speech by saying that the least individual among them is greater than the greatest individual in the clan of Abi-ezer, of which he is one, so that the least work they did against the Midianites is greater in worth than the greatest work accomplished by him and his clan. By this his longsuffering appears, for he did not rebuke them for having yielded for seven years to the humiliation of the Midianites, but encouraged them and thanked them, to heal their pride or their smallness of soul and win their love by his humility.

8.2.0.en: Their anger was abated (their spirit was relaxed): their souls grew calm.

8.2.1.en: The Lord has given you to defeat the two princes of the Midianites, "Oreb and Zeeb", and to capture them and kill them, and this was among the most important causes of achieving the final victory over the Midianite army. Then he asked: What have I done like you? Your contribution to achieving the victory cannot be compared with my work of little value.

8.2.2.en: For Gideon regarded the blowing of the trumpets and the breaking of the pitchers as a small work, while Ephraim's pursuit of the fugitives and the killing of the two princes was a very great work, and by this he calmed the souls of the tribe of Ephraim and removed their anger against him.

8.2.3.en: By this gentle speech and great humility Gideon was able to calm the intensity of the anger of the tribe of Ephraim against him, so their souls grew calm and the fires of anger were quenched. So be longsuffering when others are angry with you, and by your humility and love you can calm them and win them, turning them by your praise of them from enemies into friends.

8.2.4.en: (2) The disobedience of the men of Succoth and Penuel and their punishment (vv. 4-17) 4 And Gideon came to Jordan, and passed over, he, and the three hundred men that were with him, faint, yet pursuing them. 5 And he said unto the men of Succoth, Give, I pray you, loaves of bread unto the people that are with me; for they be faint, and I am pursuing after Zebah and Zalmunna, kings of Midian. 6 And the princes of Succoth said, Are the hands of Zebah and Zalmunna now in thine hand, that we should give bread unto thine army? 7 And Gideon said, Therefore when the Lord hath delivered Zebah and Zalmunna into mine hand, then I will thresh your flesh with the thorns of the wilderness and with threshing instruments. 8 And he went up thence to Penuel, and spake unto them likewise: and the men of Penuel answered him as the men of Succoth had answered him. 9 And he spake also unto the men of Penuel, saying, When I come again in peace, I will break down this tower. 10 Now Zebah and Zalmunna were in Karkor, and their hosts with them, about fifteen thousand men, all that were left of all the hosts of the children of the east: for there fell an hundred and twenty thousand men that drew sword. 11 And Gideon went up by the way of them that dwelt in tents on the east of Nobah and Jogbehah, and smote the host: for the host was secure. 12 And when Zebah and Zalmunna fled, he pursued after them, and took the two kings of Midian, Zebah and Zalmunna, and discomfited all the host. 13 And Gideon the son of Joash returned from battle from the ascent of Heres.

8.2.5.en: 14 And caught a young man of the men of Succoth, and enquired of him: and he wrote for him the princes of Succoth, and the elders thereof, even threescore and seventeen men. 15 And he came unto the men of Succoth, and said, Behold Zebah and Zalmunna, with whom ye did upbraid me, saying, Are the hands of Zebah and Zalmunna now in thine hand, that we should give bread unto thy men that are weary? 16 And he took the elders of the city, and thorns of the wilderness and threshing instruments, and with them he taught the men of Succoth. 17 And he beat down the tower of Penuel, and slew the men of the city.

8.3.0.en: Gideon and his men crossed the Jordan to the eastern bank to pursue the fugitives among the enemies who had succeeded in crossing the river. His men, as they pursued the fleeing enemies, had become very weary from the effort they had put forth in the war against the Midianites.

8.4.0.en: Succoth: a city about 6 km east of the Jordan River in the portion of the tribe of Gad, lying north of the river Jabbok. The meaning of its name is booths, because Jacob made booths for himself when he settled in it (Gen 33:17) (Map 12). Gideon and his men reached a town called Succoth, and they were weary and hungry. So Gideon asked the men of Succoth to give food to the men with him so that they might satisfy their hunger and be able to continue their march in pursuit of the two kings of the Midianites, "Zebah and Zalmunna", in order to seize them and kill them as a recompense for the evils they had committed against the people of Israel.

8.5.0.en: The men of Succoth replied to him coldly, saying to him: Have you actually seized Zebah and Zalmunna so that they are under your control? This was mockery of him on their part, for they saw the smallness of his army and made light of him and the men with him, believing that he and his few men could not do anything. Perhaps the refusal of the men of Succoth to help Gideon and his men was due to:

8.5.2.en: 2- The existence of interests between them and their neighbors the Midianites, or their fear of the Midianites, and their not fearing God and their distance from His worship.

8.6.0.en: Threshing instruments: the plural of "norag", a cart that runs on wheels, consisting of knives that cut the stalks of wheat after it is harvested in preparation for separating the grain from the straw, and this is called the process of threshing. Just as the grain is mixed with the straw, Gideon would mix the flesh of the men of Succoth with the thorns of the desert when he threshed them with the threshing instrument, that is, he would kill them and cut up their flesh.

8.6.1.en: Gideon was confident that the Lord would deliver his enemies Zebah and Zalmunna into his hand, and he warned the men of Succoth of the punishment with which he threatened them when that happened, that he would thresh their flesh with the thorns of the wilderness with threshing instruments, because he considered their words not merely an insult to his person but to the Lord, because they doubted the Lord's giving him victory.

8.7.0.en: Penuel: the meaning of its name is the face of God, and it lies east of the city of Succoth which is east of the Jordan, and in it Jacob saw God and wrestled with Him (Gen 32:30). Gideon and his small army continued to march until they reached the next city after Succoth, at a short distance, which is "Penuel", and he asked its people the same request that he had previously made of the men of Succoth, which was that they give food to his men, and they also refused.

8.8.0.en: Gideon's reply to the answer of the men of Penuel carried the meaning of complete confidence in the Lord's victory and in his returning in peace after accomplishing his mission. Then he threatened them with the throwing down of the tower in which the men of Penuel took refuge in time of danger.

8.9.0.en: Karkor: a city of the Midianites lying east of the Jordan.

8.9.1.en: The two kings of the Midianites, "Zebah and Zalmunna", were in "Karkor" and with them what remained of the army, 15 thousand, the army which was made up of the Midianites and the Amalekites and their allies from the peoples living east of the Jordan and east of the Red Sea.

8.9.2.en: The number of men of this army at the outbreak of the fighting was 135 thousand, of whom 120 thousand were killed by Gideon and his men, and there remained only 15 thousand bearers of arms.

8.10.0.en: Nobah: one of the cities of the tribe of Gad east of Gilead.

8.10.1.en: Jogbehah: it lies northwest of Amman at about 9.5 km.

8.10.2.en: Gideon did not take the usual road to reach Karkor, but chose another road on both sides of which nomadic groups lived. So his arrival at Karkor was a surprise to the two kings "Zebah and Zalmunna", for they were at ease and never expected him to arrive by this road. The surprise caused confusion in the ranks of the army of the two kings, so it was scattered after most of it was killed, and the two kings found no recourse but to flee.

8.10.3.en: Our confession that God is the One who works and orders our lives must not deter us from putting forth our effort in planning our lives and arranging our affairs. Here is Gideon, who, having become certain of the Lord's will to give him victory, did not lean on dependence and laziness but began to make plans that would guarantee him the achievement of this victory: there was the idea of the empty pitchers, the torches and the blowing of the trumpets, as came in the previous chapter, as was also his plan to reach Karkor by way of the dwellers in tents. We must share in the work with the Lord, even with our little effort, and the Lord completes.

8.11.0.en: The two kings fled, but Gideon overtook them and captured them after causing great confusion in the ranks of their army and destroying most of its fighters.

8.12.0.en: The ascent of Heres: a high city beside a mountain called Heres lying east of the Jordan. Gideon and his men returned victorious with "Zebah and Zalmunna" as captives in his grasp, and reached Succoth, passing through a region called the ascent of Heres.

8.13.0.en: Gideon seized a young man of the men of Succoth and asked him to write a list of the names of the princes of the city and its elders, and their number was seventy-seven men.

8.14.0.en: Gideon entered the city of Succoth and spoke to its people and showed them Zebah and Zalmunna, whom the Lord had delivered into his hand so that they had become captives with him, and reminded them of their failure to respond to his request when he asked them for bread for his men while he was on his way to fight the two kings, and reminded them of their insulting reply, full of mockery and doubt of his ability to face the enemy, and even doubt of the ability of God.

8.15.0.en: And with them he taught the men of Succoth: he gave them a lesson by this so that they would not repeat their mistake again.

8.15.1.en: Gideon carried out what he had threatened the people of the city with: he took the great men of the city and made them lie down on the thorns that he spread under them, and then had the threshing instruments tread them, and killed them in the worst way, making them an example to those who let down their brothers, and he disciplined the people of that city by what he did to their elders, who were the cause of the refusal to help Gideon and of stirring up the people of the city against him.

8.16.0.en: Gideon also carried out what he had threatened the people of the city of Penuel with: he threw down the tower in which they had fortified themselves and killed the men of the city.

8.16.1.en: The men of Succoth and Penuel tried to weaken the resolve of Gideon and his men, and their punishment was death. So do not cast doubt on the work of others, but encourage everyone to bear afflictions and overcome failure by the power of God, and He will bless you and give you victory in all your steps.

8.16.2.en: (3) Gideon kills the kings of Midian (vv. 18-21) 18 Then said he unto Zebah and Zalmunna, What manner of men were they whom ye slew at Tabor? And they answered, As thou art, so were they; each one resembled the children of a king. 19 And he said, They were my brethren, even the sons of my mother: as the Lord liveth, if ye had saved them alive, I would not slay you. 20 And he said unto Jether his firstborn, Up, and slay them. But the youth drew not his sword: for he feared, because he was yet a youth. 21 Then Zebah and Zalmunna said, Rise thou, and fall upon us: for as the man is, so is his strength. And Gideon arose, and slew Zebah and Zalmunna, and took away the ornaments that were on their camels' necks.

8.17.0.en: The Midianites' oppression of the children of Israel was not limited to seizing their crops, their cattle and their money, but went beyond that to the killing of the elite of their men and youths, out of a desire to wipe out the young men of the people of God and deprive their people of them. And here Gideon reminds them of their killing of his brothers at "Tabor" in the days of their domination over the children of Israel. And the two kings confessed to killing the excellent young men, describing them as having been in the beauty and strength of the sons of kings.

8.18.0.en: He told them who those young men were, that they were his brothers by his father and mother, and showed them that had they spared the lives of his brothers, he would pardon them now.

8.19.0.en: He drew not his sword: he unsheathes or draws his sword from its scabbard to kill.

8.19.1.en: Gideon commanded his firstborn son "Jether" to kill them, but the boy did not dare because of his youth. Gideon wanted a youth to kill them in order to humiliate them.

8.20.0.en: Fall upon us: stand yourself and kill us with your own hand.

8.20.1.en: As the man is, so is his strength: you are a strong man and can kill us with one strong stroke of the sword.

8.20.2.en: Ornaments (crescents): the plural of crescent, and they were made of gold or silver.

8.20.3.en: The two kings of the Midianites asked Gideon to kill them himself, because if the youth killed them he would not have the strength to cut off their heads with the first stroke of the sword, which would prolong and increase the pain of the two kings, while for Gideon one stroke of his sword was sufficient, and thus their pains would be less. In addition to that, it was an honor for them to be killed by the commander rather than by any soldier or youth. And after he killed them he took the golden and silver crescents which they hung on the necks of their camels for ornament.

8.20.4.en: The two kings were cruel in their killing of the young men of the great ones at Tabor, and that was the reason for their being killed. So do not be hasty in cruel or unjust acts lest they come upon you and God punish you with the same deeds, but be merciful and you will obtain mercy from God.

8.20.5.en: (4) Gideon refuses to rule over the people but makes an ephod (vv. 22-28) 22 Then the men of Israel said unto Gideon, Rule thou over us, both thou, and thy son, and thy son's son also: for thou hast delivered us from the hand of Midian. 23 And Gideon said unto them, I will not rule over you, neither shall my son rule over you: the Lord shall rule over you. 24 And Gideon said unto them, I would desire a request of you, that ye would give me every man the earrings of his prey. (For they had golden earrings, because they were Ishmaelites.) 25 And they answered, We will willingly give them. And they spread a garment, and did cast therein every man the earrings of his prey. 26 And the weight of the golden earrings that he requested was a thousand and seven hundred shekels of gold; beside ornaments, and collars, and purple raiment that was on the kings of Midian, and beside the chains that were about their camels' necks. 27 And Gideon made an ephod thereof, and put it in his city, even in Ophrah: and all Israel went thither a whoring after it: which thing became a snare unto Gideon, and to his house. 28 Thus was Midian subdued before the children of Israel, so that they lifted up their heads no more. And the country was in quietness forty years in the days of Gideon.

8.21.0.en: In acknowledgment of Gideon's merit toward the children of Israel, and out of loyalty on their part to the one who delivered them from slavery to the Midianites, they offered him that he and his descendants after him should rule over them. This was in imitation of the nations surrounding them, because God was the One who ruled over the children of Israel, and they did not set up kings until later, in the days of Samuel, when he made Saul king (1 Sam 8:5, 10:24).

8.22.0.en: Gideon was humble in his request and was not deluded by the victory he had achieved, so he was content to have brought them deliverance and was not covetous of kingship or authority, but reminded the people that he was only a mediator in achieving this deliverance, which was from the Lord alone, and He is worthy to rule over them. This shows Gideon's piety and humility, for he believes that God is the leader and king over His people and he did not exploit the people's submission to him to steal God's glory.

8.22.1.en: Beware of stealing God's glory when others praise you, but ascribe the glory to Him, and do not exploit the need or weakness of others to domineer over them, and know that you and they are servants of God; that is, be humble however much Satan adorns for you an opportunity for boasting and pride.

8.23.0.en: Earrings: the plural of earring, that which is worn in the ear for adornment.

8.23.1.en: His prey: what the children of Israel took as spoil from the Midianites.

8.23.2.en: They had: that is, the Midianites had.

8.23.3.en: Gideon asked the people to give him the golden earrings they had taken as spoil from the Midianites. For it was the custom of the Midianites that their women, and sometimes their men also, wore golden earrings in imitation of the Ishmaelites, with whom they had mingled by intermarriage and trade, for the Midianites are the descendants of Keturah, the wife of Abraham, and not the descendants of Ishmael.

8.24.0.en: When the children of Israel saw Gideon's humility and his renunciation of kingship, they did not hesitate for a moment to meet his request to collect the earrings, so they spread a garment on the ground and each of them cast in the golden earrings they had taken as spoil from the Midianites.

8.25.0.en: Collars (necklaces): the plural of necklace, that which a person wears around his neck.

8.25.2.en: The weight of the golden earrings that were collected was about 25 kg, which shows the wealth of the Midianites; this is apart from the golden crescents that were hung on the camels and horses and the jewelry made in the form of rings (anklets and necklaces), and the splendid garments of colored purple cloth belonging to the Midianite kings and chiefs, and also the golden collars which they placed around the necks of the camels as a kind of adornment and boasting of wealth.

8.26.0.en: All Israel went a whoring after it: they left the worship of the Lord and worshiped the ephod that Gideon had made.

8.26.1.en: Which thing became a snare unto Gideon and to his house: the matter of the ephod was a cause that brought Gideon and the people of his house into troubles.

8.26.2.en: The ephod: a short garment covering the chest, which was part of the garments of the high priest, worn when he judged the people, to give him awe and dignity. Samuel and David used to do the same thing on certain occasions (1 Chr 15:27). Gideon made an ephod of splendid cloth and adorned it with the gold he had collected from the people.

8.26.3.en: And he put the ephod in his city of Ophrah, and his intention in making the ephod was good, but matters came out the opposite way, for it was a stumbling block to the people, since they left the worship of the Lord and the ephod dazzled them with its golden gleam, so they worshiped it as they had done before with the golden calf during their exodus from Egypt to Sinai.

8.26.4.en: The people's falling into the worship of the ephod grieved Gideon and the people of his house, and perhaps some of them turned aside to conceit and pride and the seeking of leadership and authority, which led Abimelech, one of the sons of Gideon, to start his movement, whose victims were seventy sons of Gideon (chs. 9, 10).

8.27.0.en: The victory of the children of Israel over the Midianites humbled them, while the children of Israel held up their heads throughout the period Gideon spent as judge of his people, a period of 40 years, so the people rested from the oppressions of the Midianites and from the acts of plunder, pillage and killing that they used to commit.

8.27.1.en: (5) The death of Gideon (vv. 29-35) 29 And Jerubbaal the son of Joash went and dwelt in his own house. 30 And Gideon had threescore and ten sons of his body begotten: for he had many wives. 31 And his concubine that was in Shechem, she also bare him a son, whose name he called Abimelech. 32 And Gideon the son of Joash died in a good old age, and was buried in the sepulchre of Joash his father, in Ophrah of the Abi-ezrites. 33 And it came to pass, as soon as Gideon was dead, that the children of Israel turned again, and went a whoring after Baalim, and made Baal-berith their god. 34 And the children of Israel remembered not the Lord their God, who had delivered them out of the hands of all their enemies on every side: 35 Neither shewed they kindness to the house of Jerubbaal (Gideon), according to all the goodness which he had shewed unto Israel.

8.28.0.en: After his struggle that was crowned with victory, Jerubbaal, which is the other name of Gideon, returned to dwell in Ophrah his city to carry out the task of judge for his people.

8.29.0.en: Of his body begotten: that is, from his own descendants and not by adoption.

8.29.1.en: Gideon had many wives, as was the case with many in those ages, and he begot seventy sons by them.

8.30.0.en: Gideon had a concubine whom he took as a wife in addition to his other original wives, and who was considered, according to the traditions of that age, to be of lower standing than the original wife; his concubine bore him a son whom he called "Abimelech."

8.31.0.en: After a long struggle and good service, Gideon died and was buried in the tomb of his father Joash in the city of Ophrah, in which lived the clan of Abiezer to which Gideon belonged.

8.32.0.en: Once again the people of God return and forget what the Lord had done for them and His rescuing them from the hand of the Midianites.

8.32.1.en: For as soon as Gideon died, they betrayed the Lord and worshiped false gods, imitating the pagan peoples by giving names to these gods, so they called the god whom the people of Shechem worshiped "Baal-berith", that is, "lord of the covenant" or "master of the covenant", as if they had made a covenant with him.

8.33.0.en: They forgot the Lord their God and did not remember His great works repeatedly done with them when He rescued them from their enemies such as the Midianites.

8.34.0.en: The people denied the Lord and also denied Gideon, who had done them a great kindness and delivered them from the Midianites, and they did not preserve gratitude toward him and his family, for they did not intervene afterward, as we shall see in the following chapters, to prevent the killing of his seventy sons, but even took part in this wicked and cruel deed to please his son Abimelech.

8.34.1.en: Hold fast to the teachings of your fathers and teachers even if they have died, for they are an example to you and taught you God's commandments. So do not be negligent of them, and know that they look at you from heaven and pray for you that you may live uprightly before God. The reign of Abimelech son of Gideon
